paras: The lynching of Wash Allen took place in DeSoto Parish, Louisiana, in July 1881, when thirty or forty masked men took Allen, a Black man jailed at Mansfield on suspicion of murdering the Kingston merchant M. J. (Judd) Scott, and hanged him at Kingston. Allen was reported to have confessed and named four or five other Black men, but a later Shreveport Times item said the confession was extorted and that the men he named proved an alibi. The hanging ran as a one-line wire item across the country, while a Mansfield correspondent wrote that local citizens approved it.

Scott, a merchant and police juror at Kingston, about twelve miles northeast of Mansfield, was shot about 9 o'clock on Saturday night, July 16, and his store was robbed. Sheriff Sample arrested two Black men on what the Shreveport Standard called strong circumstantial evidence and on Monday sent them to the Mansfield jail. According to the Minden Democrat, Scott's watch and clothing and a pair of bloodstained pants were found at Allen's house. The Standard reported a rumored attempt to take the prisoners from the sheriff "for the purpose of lynching" and warned that the people would be hard to restrain.

On the night of Monday, July 18, thirty or forty armed and masked men came to the Mansfield jail. The Minden Democrat said they roused the deputy sheriff by claiming to have a prisoner to lock up, then overpowered him and took the key; the Mansfield correspondent wrote that the keys were forced from the jailer. They took out Allen, one of the two prisoners, carried him back to Kingston and hanged him, by the correspondent's account about daylight on July 19, from a tree opposite Scott's store or, in the Minden version, a limb a few yards from where Scott was killed.

Citing the Mansfield stage driver, the Times reported that Allen made "a clean breast" of the crime, said four or five others had stood guard while he fired, and showed where the gun was hidden. A later Times item said instead that he had been "swung up sixteen or eighteen times" to extort a confession and told "a disconnected story."

The men Allen named were arrested on Tuesday and jailed at Mansfield, where lynching them was "freely talked of" while the sheriff's deputies guarded them. No report of a further lynching appears in the coverage, and the later Times item said those implicated "clearly proved an alibi." The lynchers were not named; the Mansfield correspondent called them men of "coolness and deliberation" from around Kingston whose action was approved "in toto" in Mansfield. No report of an inquest, an arrest of any lyncher or a trial was found.

The news reached national papers on July 20 as a one-sentence dispatch, and several placed the lynching "at Shreveport," the dateline, rather than at Mansfield. A St. Louis Republican special called Allen "a negro murderer" taken by "forty armed maskers," and the Chicago Tribune headed its item "Hanged by a Mob." A second wire brief, run by weeklies from Arkansas to Kansas into August, stated as fact that Allen "murdered" Scott, and the Somerset Press in Ohio headed its version "Doing Away With Expenses."

In Louisiana, the Capitolian reprinted the Times report as "A Full Confession Made by Wash Allen, Whose Case, Was Disposed of by Judge Lynch," with the Mansfield letter calling it "idle to talk or think of the slow process of the law." The Times predicted "swift and just punishment" for the other prisoners, and the Lake Charles Echo claimed "positive proof" against the man hanged. The Times's later item, which the Evening Star in Washington headed "The Horrors of Lynch Law," reported the extorted confession while still calling Allen a "hardened wretch."

The wires had Allen hanged the night he was taken, the Mansfield letter about daylight on July 19, and other items "the 20th" or Tuesday night; the letter, written locally that day, is the closest account. Both versions of the confession come from the Times: the first had Allen naming accomplices and leading the party to the gun, the later one had him hoisted repeatedly until he implicated men who proved an alibi.

accounts.label: Shreveport Times, first report
accounts.gist: Allen made a full confession implicating four or five others, whose lynching was expected, and showed where the bloodied gun was hidden.

framing.detail: National dailies ran one-sentence items calling Allen 'a negro murderer' taken by 'forty armed maskers', the Chicago Tribune under 'Hanged by a Mob'.
The Mansfield letter called the lynchers 'gentlemen' of 'coolness and deliberation' and dismissed 'the slow process of the law'; the Times called the hanging 'swift and just punishment'.
The later Times item, run by the Evening Star as 'The Horrors of Lynch Law', reported the extorted confession and the alibi while still calling Allen a 'hardened wretch'.
The wire brief in rural weeklies stated that Allen 'murdered' Scott; the Somerset Press headed it 'Doing Away With Expenses'.

versions.value: Hanged the night of Monday, July 18 ('last night' in July 19 wires)

conflicts.note: The Mansfield letter, dated July 19 and written locally, is the best evidence: seized Monday night, hanged at daybreak July 19. The 20th and Tuesday-night versions are summary or wire errors.
